This lesson teaches the common emitter amplifier circuit.
INTRODUCTIONM
This is a Common Emitter amplifier because the input is applied to the base, the output is taken from the collector, and the emitter is common.
The common emitter amplifier is normally used as a power amplifier due to its properties.
Voltage Gain - Medium Current Gain - Medium Power Gain - High Input Resistance - Medium Output Resistance - Medium

DISCUSSION
For this discussion an NPN transistor is used. Note that Vcc is positive.
The amplifier's output is controlled by a small input signal.
The output signal is an amplified and inverted replica of the input signal.
2. Output - Emitter to Collectorrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrr
Note, the emitter is common to both circuits.
This means that a change in one circuit affects the other circuit.
A changing input signal changes the bias voltage on the base of the transistor.
When the input signal increases, the bias voltage increases.
An increase in bias voltage affects current flow in the emitter collector circuit. Current increases.
When the input signal decreases, the bias voltage decreases.
A decrease in bias voltage affects current flow in the emitter collector circuit. Current decreases.
The effects of a changing input signal are seen in a changing output signal.
Note, an increasing input signal produces a decreasing output signal.
A decreasing input signal produces an increasing output signal.
A small input signal controlled a large output signal.
In a common emitter amplifier, when the base voltage increases the emitter current _______
When the base voltage increases, the forward biased emitter to base PN junction increases. Emitter current will not decrease.

R1 and R2 form a voltage divider that is operated by +Vcc. A fixed bias is always present on the base of Q1..
Any change in the fixed bias of Q1 produces a predicted change at the output.
Resistor R4 and bypass capacitor C1 provide self biasing or stability for the circuit.
Normal operation of the amplifier produces heat. Heat causes an unpredictable change at the output.
R4 provides temperature stability by decreasing emitter current when current increases due to heat.
R4 provides temperature stability by decreasing emitter current when current increases due to heat...
DEFINITION

TEMPERATURE STABILITY - If the temperature of the transistor increases the emitter current increases. This causes the voltage drop across R4 to increase, decreasing the forward bias between the base and emitter decreasing emitter current.
C1 provides a path for any unwanted AC that is produced. This insures that the output signal is not affected..
C1 provides a path for any unwanted AC that is produced. This insures that the output signal is not affected.
UNWANTED AC - The value of the bypass capacitor allows a low reactance to the frequency of the input signal. The changing emitter voltage, due to the input signal, is shorted to ground.
DEFINITION

The bypass capacitor also has a high reactance to very low frequencies. This prevents a voltage change on the emitter, due to a temperature change, from being grounded. Temperature changes are normally slow or low frequency.
DEFINITION
The output signal is determined by collector load resistor R3.
When the emitter to collector current increases, more voltage drops across R3 and the output signal decreases.
When current decreases, less voltage is dropped across R3 and the output signal increases.
The result is a signal on the output that is a replica of the input signal except it is amplified and inverted.
Now, let's add two important components to the amplifier circuit, C2 and C3.
C2 is an input coupling capacitor that prevents any DC voltage from the input, from reaching the base of the transistor..
C3 is an output coupling capacitor that prevents the DC bias on the collector from reaching the output.
The coupling capacitors do not effect the bias voltages on Q1.
